prompt: The section subtracts the equilibrium relation 0 = Δ_r G° + RT ln K from Δ_r G = Δ_r G° + RT ln Q. What does it get?

choices.text: Δ_r G = RT ln(Q/K)
Δ_r G = RT ln(K/Q)
choices.why: The ratio is upside down: RT ln Q − RT ln K = RT ln(Q/K). With K/Q, a mixture short of products would get a positive Δ_r G.

choices.text: Δ_r G = Δ_r G° + RT ln(Q/K)
choices.why: Subtracting removes Δ_r G°, since it appears in both relations. What remains is Δ_r G = RT ln(Q/K).

choices.text: Δ_r G = RT ln(Q × K)
choices.why: Subtracting logarithms divides their arguments: ln Q − ln K = ln(Q/K). So Δ_r G = RT ln(Q/K).

explanation: Δ_r G − 0 = (Δ_r G° − Δ_r G°) + RT ln Q − RT ln K, so Δ_r G = RT ln(Q/K). The sign of Δ_r G now depends only on whether Q is smaller or larger than K.

prompt: According to the section, what is the main difference between the equilibrium constant K and the reaction quotient Q?

choices.text: K is at equilibrium; Q is at any moment
K uses pressures; Q uses concentrations
choices.why: Either can be written with pressures or concentrations. The difference is that K uses the equilibrium values and Q the values present now.

choices.text: Q is always the inverse of K
choices.why: Q has the same form as K, products over reactants, not the inverse. It uses the current amounts instead of the equilibrium ones.

choices.text: K changes during the reaction; Q does not
choices.why: It is the other way round: Q changes as the reaction proceeds until it reaches K, which is fixed at a given temperature.

explanation: Q has the same form as K, products over reactants with coefficients as powers, but it uses the concentrations or pressures actually present. Only at equilibrium does Q equal K.

prompt: For 2NO(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g), which expression is the reaction quotient Q, written with concentrations?

choices.why: This is upside down. Q puts the products in the numerator and the reactants in the denominator.
The coefficients are missing. Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient, so [NO2] and [NO] are squared.
Coefficients become powers, not factors, and the reactant terms multiply rather than add.

explanation: Q multiplies the product terms and divides by the reactant terms, each raised to the power of its coefficient. Here that gives Q = ([NO2]^2)/([NO]^2 [O2]).

prompt: A reaction mixture has Q > K. According to the section, which way does the reaction shift?

choices.text: To the left, making more reactants
To the right, making more products
choices.why: Q > K means the product-to-reactant ratio is already above its equilibrium value. Making more products would push Q further from K.

choices.text: It does not shift; it is already at equilibrium
choices.why: Equilibrium needs Q = K. With Q > K, the reaction runs in reverse until Q falls to K.

choices.text: To the left, until no products remain
choices.why: The reaction shifts left only until Q = K, not until the products are gone. At that point equilibrium is reached.

explanation: Q > K means there are more products relative to reactants than at equilibrium. The excess products turn back into reactants, so the reaction shifts left until Q = K.

prompt: For CO(g) + Cl2(g) ⇌ COCl2(g), K = 10 at some temperature. A mixture has P_(COCl2) = 0.200 bar, P_(CO) = 0.400 bar and P_(Cl2) = 0.100 bar, and Q = (P_(COCl2))/(P_(CO) P_(Cl2)), with pressures in bar. Which way does the reaction go?

choices.text: Forward, making more COCl2
In reverse, making more CO and Cl2
choices.why: Q = 0.200/(0.400 × 0.100) = 5.0, which is below K = 10. The reaction makes more product until Q = K.

choices.text: Neither way; it is at equilibrium
choices.why: Equilibrium needs Q = K, but Q = 5.0 here, below K = 10. The reaction still runs forward.

choices.text: Forward, until all the CO is used up
choices.why: The reaction runs forward, but only until Q reaches K = 10. Some CO and Cl2 remain at equilibrium.

explanation: Q = 0.200/(0.400 × 0.100) = 5.0, which is less than K = 10. There are too few products relative to reactants, so the reaction shifts right, forming COCl2 until Q = K.

prompt: For CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O in a liquid mixture, K = 4.0. A mixture has [CH3COOC2H5] = [H2O] = 0.600 M and [CH3COOH] = [C2H5OH] = 0.300 M. What will happen?

choices.text: No net change; the mixture is at equilibrium
It reacts forward, since products exceed reactants
choices.why: Having more products than reactants does not by itself cause a shift. Q = (0.600 × 0.600)/(0.300 × 0.300) = 4.0 = K.

choices.text: It reacts in reverse, since products exceed reactants
choices.why: A shift to the left needs Q > K. Here Q = 4.0, exactly K, so there is no tendency to change.

choices.text: It reacts forward until the acid is used up
choices.why: Q already equals K = 4.0, so there is no drive forward. The mixture is at equilibrium.

explanation: Q = (0.600 × 0.600)/(0.300 × 0.300) = 0.360/0.0900 = 4.0, equal to K. With Q = K, Δ_r G = RT ln 1 = 0, so neither more reactants nor more products form.

prompt: For a reaction with K = 100, a mixture has Q = 10. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It shifts right, though products may outnumber reactants
It shifts right, because there are more reactants than products
choices.why: Q = 10 means the product-to-reactant ratio is 10, so products can outnumber reactants. Q < K says only that this ratio is below its equilibrium value.

choices.text: It shifts left, because Q is smaller than K
choices.why: Q < K means too few products relative to equilibrium. The reaction shifts right, making more products.

choices.text: It is at equilibrium, since both Q and K exceed 1
choices.why: Equilibrium needs Q = K, not just both above 1. Here Q = 10 is below K = 100, so the reaction shifts right.

explanation: Q < K, so the reaction shifts right to make more products. But Q = 10 already means a product-to-reactant ratio of 10: Q < K says only that the ratio is below its equilibrium value, not that reactants are in excess.

prompt: A reaction mixture starts with Q > K. As the reaction proceeds, what happens to Q?

choices.text: Q falls until it equals K
Q rises until it equals K
choices.why: With Q > K the reaction runs in reverse, using up products, so Q falls. It stops changing once Q = K.

choices.text: Q stays fixed while K falls to meet it
choices.why: K is fixed at a given temperature. It is Q, built from the changing amounts, that moves toward K.

choices.text: Q falls until it reaches zero
choices.why: Q stops falling once it equals K, because equilibrium has then been reached. Q = 0 would mean no products at all.

explanation: Running in reverse turns products into reactants, which lowers the ratio Q. The section notes that Q changes until Q = K, when equilibrium is reached.

prompt: Using Δ_r G = RT ln(Q/K), what is the sign of Δ_r G for a mixture with Q < K, and which way does it react?

choices.text: Negative; it proceeds left to right
Positive; it proceeds left to right
choices.why: Q/K < 1 makes ln(Q/K) negative, so Δ_r G < 0. A negative Δ_r G is what drives the forward reaction.

choices.text: Negative; it runs in reverse
choices.why: The sign is right, but a negative Δ_r G means the forward reaction, left to right, is spontaneous.

choices.text: Zero; it is at equilibrium
choices.why: Δ_r G = 0 needs Q/K = 1. With Q < K, ln(Q/K) < 0, so Δ_r G is negative and the reaction goes forward.

explanation: For Q < K, Q/K < 1 and ln(Q/K) < 0, so Δ_r G < 0. The section says a negative Δ_r G means the reaction proceeds spontaneously from left to right as written.

prompt: Two mixtures of the same reaction at the same temperature have Q = K/10 and Q = K/1000. Using Δ_r G = RT ln(Q/K), how do their values of Δ_r G compare?

choices.text: Both are negative, more so for Q = K/1000
Both are negative, more so for Q = K/10
choices.why: ln(1/1000) = −6.91 is more negative than ln(1/10) = −2.30. The mixture farther from equilibrium has the more negative Δ_r G.

choices.text: They are equal, since K is the same
choices.why: Δ_r G depends on Q/K, which differs by a factor of 100 between the mixtures. The one with Q = K/1000 has the more negative Δ_r G.

choices.text: Both are positive, more so for Q = K/1000
choices.why: Q/K < 1 makes ln(Q/K) negative, so both values are negative. The farther mixture, Q = K/1000, has the more negative one.

explanation: Δ_r G is RT ln(1/10) = −2.30 RT for one and RT ln(1/1000) = −6.91 RT for the other. Both mixtures react forward, and the one farther from equilibrium has the larger driving force.

prompt: For 2NOCl(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) + Cl2(g), a mixture has P_(NOCl) = 0.500 bar, P_(NO) = 0.250 bar and P_(Cl2) = 0.400 bar. Using Q = (P_(NO)^2 P_(Cl2))/(P_(NOCl)^2), with the pressures in bar (P° = 1 bar), what is Q? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Q = (0.250^2 × 0.400)/(0.500^2) = 0.0250/0.250 = 0.100. Comparing this Q with K at the same temperature tells which way the mixture will react.

prompt: A reaction at 300 K has K = 50, and a mixture of it has Q = 0.50. Using Δ_r G = RT ln(Q/K), with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and ln(0.0100) = −4.605, what is Δ_r G, in kJ/mol, including its sign? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Q/K = 0.50/50 = 0.0100, so Δ_r G = 8.314 × 300 × (−4.605) J/mol = 2494 × (−4.605) J/mol = −11486 J/mol, or −11.5 kJ/mol. The negative sign means the mixture reacts forward, as Q < K requires.
